There seems to be a growing acknowledgement around the word that Keynes was right when he proposed at Bretton Woods a global trading regime that limited persistent trade imbalances and restricted global financial flows.

In her new Foreign Affairs piece, Lori Wallach proposes a similar restructuring of the global trading regime, arguing that because our current trading system rewards countries that improve their manufacturing competitiveness by suppressing wage growth relative to productivity growth (and by ignoring environmental costs), it's no surprise that income inequality has risen across most countries over the past four decades.

Like a growing number of analysts, she argues that countries should be free to choose their own growth models, but they should not be able to externalize the associated costs via their trade and capital accounts.

For years while economists both inside and outside China have called on Beijing to fight off delation and raise the consumption share of GDP by lowering interest rates and expanding credit, I have argued that this is the wrong solution, based on mistakenly assuming that China's financial system works like that of the US.

In fact it works in a very different way. Chinese banks mostly borrow from households to lend to businesses and government. Households are overwhelmingly net creditors to the banks while businesses and government net borrowers.

Lowering interest rates, in other words, rather mechanically reduces the household income share of GDP and expand the business and government shares, which means it tends to expand production faster than consumption.

We saw this most obviously in the 2000s, when Beijing engineered highly negative real interest rates to help clean up bad debt, and saw a near-collapse of the household share of GDP (and with it, the consumption share).

That's why, I argued, credit expansion and lower interest rates in China actually reduce consumption and are likely to be deflationary. This, by the way, was a similar story in Japan in the 1980s and 1990s.

Jinfan Zhang and Wei Xiong have just published an NBER paper that makes a very similar point. They write: "This paper investigates why China’s recurrent credit expansions have coincided with persistently weak inflation. We argue that this pattern reflects the country’s production-oriented monetary regime."

"Credit expansion in China," they continue, "tends to sustain production and balance sheets rather than stimulate final demand. As a result, monetary policy operates less as a conventional tool for demand management and durable reflation, and more as a mechanism for preserving production capacity and supporting growth."

If they are right (and I think they clearly are right), this has the seemingly counter-intuitive implication that rebalancing the economy towards a greater reliance on domestic consumption requires higher, not lower interest rates.

Of course given how heavily indebted government and businesses are, raising interest rates will be extremely painful for the production side of the economy, but this simply reinforces what we already know from the historical precedents – that it is necessary, but extremely painful, to rebalance an economy with very low consumption.

That's because the income transfers needed to rebalance an economy towards consumption must come from a production side that had previously benefitted from the reverse transfers. This almost always results in a growth contraction on the production side. That is probably why rebalancing is always put off for so long.

I think John Burn-Murdoch is right: "The most durable way for governments to ensure that both university students and their less academic counterparts can move through the education system confident of good financial outcomes for themselves is to have a dynamic economy and robust productivity growth."

You hear all sorts of silly arguments that China has a strong manufacturing sector because its universities produce engineers, where American universities produces lawyers, but this is the same sort of silliness we heard about Japan in the 1980s, and, just as it did then, it gets the causality backwards.

Chinese students – like Japanese students in the 1980s, Germans in the 2000s and Americans in the 1950s and 1960s – major in engineering because, thanks to the tremendous support its government gives to the manufacturing and high-tech sectors, that is where the best jobs are. If the UK and the US want the same, instead of prioritizing finance and services, they should prioritize manufacturing. Once the opportunities are there, the students will follow.

There's probably no need to point out that China's July trade numbers would have seemed extraordinary just five or six years ago. Exports and imports were both up year on year by roughly a quarter. China's trade surplus in July was $112.5 billion, the sixth largest monthly trade surplus ever recorded. Among the larger surpluses, all occurred in China, with three in 2025 and two so far in 2026.

Year to date China's trade surplus is $693 billion, versus $685 in 2025, $522 in 2024, $512 in 2023, and $491 in 2022. It is on track to exceed last year's $1.2 trillion, which will make it roughly 5.8% of China's GDP and 1.2% of the GDP of the rest of the world.
